is readily available with the State Governments und er the Calamity Relief 
Fund to enable them to take necessary relief measur es in the wake of natural 
calamities resulting in destruction of crops. Gover nment of India and State

†*168. SHRI AMIR ALAM KHAN: Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be 
pleased to state: 
(a)the purpose of Government behind running the Garib Rath Express 
trains; 
(b)whether it is a fact that these trains are not even able to recover their 
operational cost due to thousands of seats remaining unoccupied; 
(c) the average number of passengers travelling by Garib Raths every 
month; 
(d)the methodology being adopted by Government to compensate the 
revenue loss caused due to unoccupied seats; 
(e)the incentives being given by Government to encourage passengers for 
travelling by Garib Raths; and 
(f) whether Government are still considering to start two more 'Garib 
Raths' despite incurring loss? 
THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS (SHRI LALU PRASAD): (a) To  
provide afforedable air-conditioned service to passengers to long distance 
trains. 
(b) No, Sir. However, train-wise profitability is n ot maintained by the 
Indian Railways. 
(c) Approximately 30,000. 
(d) Does not arise. However, suitable reduction/augmentation of coaches 
in trains is a regular exercise being done by Indian Railways. 
(e) Nil, Sir. However, "Garib Rath" concept is itself is the incentive with 
low AC fare. 
(f) Already introduced. 
Electronic industries contamainating the rivers  
*169. DR. MAM. RAMASWAMY Will the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether a survey conducted by Green Peace has revealed that some of 
the biggest brands in electronics industries and their suppliers 
†Onginal notice of the question was received in Hindi 
42 

[9 March, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
are contaminating rivers and underground wells with a wide range of 
hazardous chemicals; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that some countries inclu ding China are taking 
steps to enforce a phase out of these toxic chemicals; and 
(d) if so, the steps taken by Government to minimize th e environmental 
pollution caused by e-waste? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI A. 
RAJA): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. The Greenpeace had car ried out a study on the 
environmental pollution during manufacturing of ele ctronic products in 
China, Thailand, Philippines and Mexico and no such  study was done for 
India. This study was an assessment on pollution du e to the use of some of 
the hazardous chemicals in the manufacture of elect ronic products in these 
countries. The study reveals some contamination of water bodies which, 
however, could not be attributed fully to the untis  manufacturing electronic 
products located in these countries the vicinity.    
(C) The European Union is reported to have issued a  directive "on the 
restriction of the use of certain hazardous substan ces in electrical and 
electronic equipment" which has come into force wit h effect from 1 July 
2006, imposing restrictions on the use of lead, mer cury, cadmium, 
hexavalent chromium, polybrominated bibhenyles (PBB ) and 
polybrominated diphenyl ethers (PBDE) in electronic  and electrical 
equipment. 
(D) The Government of India has taken the following ste ps to minimize 
the pollution caused by e-waste: 
 
(1) The Hazardous Wastes (Management and Handling) Rule s, 1989 as 
amended in 2000 and 2003 includes e-waste.These rul es regulate 
the generation, collection, storage, treatment, dis posal, export and 
import of all hazardous wastes. 
(2) The Department of Information Technology, Ministryo f 
Communication and Information Technology, Governmen t of India, 
has taken steps to promote adoptioon of cleaner tec hnologies and to 
motivate the electronics industry to minimize gener ation of waste. 
They have also published a comprehensive technical guide on

for wide circulation to electronics industry. 
(3) The Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) has cond cuted a study 
on the assessment of electrical and electronic wast e generation and 
have also undertaken the task on preparation of a ' Guidelines 
Document for Environmnetally Sound Recycling of E-Waste' for the 
State Pollution Control Boards and Pollution Contro l Committees of 
the Union Territories as well as the industries. 
(4) Measures have also been initiated to create awarene ss among the 
electronic industry for the adoption on cleaner pro duction 
technologies and minimization hazardous waste generation. 
Protection of crops from fungal disease  
†*170.   SHRI SATYAVRAT  HATURVEDI: 
SHRI MOTILAL VORA: 
Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of the fact that comin g out from Africa 
a type of fungus harming the wheat crop has reached  Yemen crossing the 
Red Sea and it may reach India in the coming three-four years; 
(b) if so, what measures Government are taking to prote ct the wheat crop 
from this fungus; and 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI SHARAD PAWAR): (a ) 
The African race of stem rust fungus of wheat is no t reported in India. 
Government is aware that a new race of stem rust of  wheat (Ug 99) with 
likely adverse effect on wheat crop has been traced  in Kenya and Yemen. 
The opinion of the experts of the International Mai ze and Wheat 
Improvement Centre (CIMMYT), Mexico is that the eff ect, speed and the 
route of the movement of the fungus is unpredictabl e in near future. 
Therefore, it is only an apprehension that the fung us may reach India is the 
coming three or four years. 
†Onginal notice of the question was received in Hindi 
44 

[9 March, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) A vigil is kept on the movement of this race by  Directorate of Wheat 
Research, Karnal, through International collaborati on. CIMMYT, Mexico is 
also providing regular information on the movement of this race. Indian 
Council of Agricultural Research, in collaboration with CIMMYT, Mexico 
has tested the Indian wheat cultivars in Africa, ag ainst the new pathotype 
(Ug 99) of the said disease. A number of wheat entr ies have been identified 
possessing resistance against the new race of the s tem rust fungus. This 
source of resistance will be useful for developing resistant wheat varieties 
which will prevent incidence of the new race of African fungus. 
There is a well established Plant Quarantine regula tory system in the 
country under the Destructive Insects and Pests Act , 1914, under which, 
necessary steps are taken to prevent the introducti on and spread of exotic 
pests and disease that are destructive to crops by regulating/restricting the 
import of plant materials and plant products. There  are well defined 
regulations under Plant Quarantine Order, 2003, for  the import of any plant 
material or plant product, either for propagation o r consumption purposes. 
Post entry quarantine inspection is also undertaken  to ensure that the 
imported plant material is free from any pests and disease. The plant 
quarantine regulations are implemented in the count ry through 39 Plant 
Quarantine Stations spread over sea ports, airports  and land custom stations. 
Further, a regular surveillance for pest and diseas e emergence in the country, 
is also conducted to take emergency measures, where ver required, through 
Central Integrated Pest Management Centres, Indian Council of a 
Agricultural Research and State Agricultural Departments 
(c) Question does not arise.

  *173. SHRI MAHENDRA MOHAN: Will the Minister of A GRICULTURE

(a) whether it is a fact that lack of awareness among t he farmers is a major 
cause of concern;

farmers aware of the various schemes of Government?

(c) 
1. Creating awareness among the farmers about the Gove rnment schemes 
and other related areas is an ongoing process. 
2. However, as per the Situational Assessment Survey ( SAS) carried out by 
the National Sample Survey Organization (NSSO) duri ng July, 2002 — June, 
2003, it has emerged that only about 29% of the far mers were aware of the 
Minimum Support Price (MSP) scheme.

steps in the recent past to support State's efforts  in creating greater awareness 
among the farmers. Some of the important steps are listed below:—

the Mass Media Scheme of the DAC. 
(iii) State and District level agricultural fairs a re supported by the DAC 
under the Agriculture Technology Management Agency (ATMA) 
Programme. Such fairs provide an important opportun ity for 
creating awareness on Government schemes and variet y of farm 
related activities.

through leaflets and print media.

Transmitters, 18 Regional Kendra and DD National ch annel of 
Doordarshan are broadcasting 30-minute agricultural  programmes, 
including those on Government Schemes and related s uccess stories, 
five/six days a week. State Level Monitoring Commit tee headed by

guidance to DD and AIR on programming and related aspects. 
(vi) Financial assistance is also provided to the S tates under AGRISNET 
initiative for providing improved services to the f arming community 
through use of Information and Communication Techno logy (ICT). 
Dissemination of information on Government Schemes is an 
important service listed in most of the approved AG RISNET 
projects. The Department of IT, Government of India is setting up of

1177. SHRI SITARAM YECHURY: Will the Minister of 
AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether, as per the Economic Survey, 2005, the priv ate investment in 
agriculture has substantially gone down in recent y ears from around Rs. 
38000 crores in 2001-02 to just Rs. 30500 crores in  2004-05 if so, whether 
this is because of a fall in supporting public expenditure, and 
(b) what would be its implications for the agrarian emp loyment scenario 
and the overall food security in coming years? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTUR E 
(SHRI KANTI LAL BHURIA): (a) As per the Economic Su rvey 2005-06, 
the private investment in agriculture (at 1999-2000  prices) has gone down 
from Rs. 38215 crore in 2001-02 to Rs. 30532 crore (quick estimates) in 
2004-05. The share of public investment in agricult ural gross investment 
rose from 18.2 per cent in 2001-02 to 29.2 per cent  in 2004-05 according to 
that survey.

of 9 per cent per annum, the projected employment i n agriculture would be 
about 24.5 crore in 2007 and 25.1 crore during 2012 . The overall food 
security system is strengthened with ensuring Minim um Support Prices 
(MSPs) to the farmers for production of crops. This  price support mechanism 
enables the farmers to sell their produce at remune rative prices, when market 
prices fall below the MSP level. The Targeted Publi c Distribution System 
(TPDS) targets below proverty line (BPL) population  by providing PDS 
entitlements at a price lower than that for the abo ve poverty line (APL) 
population. Other programmes like Antyodaya Anna Yo jana (AAY) are in 
operation to provide foodgrains to the poorest of t he poor households from 
the BPL.

Suicides vis-a-vis  pluse Production  
1183. SHRI RAHUL BAJAJ: Will the Minister of AGRICU LTURE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) the reasons for this paradox situation of farmers c ommitting suicides 
because of unremunerative crops and large scale imp orts and increasing 
prices of pulses during the last five years; and 
(b) if so, the reasons for which pulses can't be grown on a large scale in 
the country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTUR E 
(SHRI KANTI LAL BHURIA): (a) On the basis of variou s studies conducted 
to assess the reasons for farmers committing suicid e, the causes can broadly 
be classified as Crop failure; Indebtedness due to loan with high rate of 
interest; Drought; and Social and Economic Insecuri ty. The Minimum 
Support Prices (MSPs) announced in recent years ind icate that between 2002-
03 and 2006-07 the increase in the MSPs of Pulses h as ranged between 6.82 
percent in case of Arhar (Tur) to 18.44 percent in case of Gram. The increase 
in prices of Pulses as reflected by the Whole Price s Index (WPI) is indicative 
of the gap between domestic supply and demand, whil e the imports of pulses 
are undertaken to bridge this gap. 
(b) The area under pulses has fluctuated between 20  million hectareas to 
23 million hectares per annum during 1995-96 to 200 5-06. The increase in 
the area of a crop is dependent not merely on the MSP of that crop but also on 
the fulfillment of agro-climatic requirements of th at crop. The pulses are 
genetically low yielding and less input responsive as compared to other crops 
like cereals, millets and oilseeds. However, the Go vernment is implementing 
a Centrally Sponsored "Integrated Scheme of Oilseed s, Pulses, Oilplam and 
Maize" (ISOPOM) in 14 major pulses growing states w ith a view to increase 
the production and productivity of Pulses. Under th e scheme assistance is 
provided to farmers for purchase of breeder seed, p roduction of foundation 
seed, production and distribution of certified seed , distribution of seed 
minikrts, plant protection chemicals and equipments , weedicides, supply of 
rhizobium culture/phosphate solubilising bacteria, distribution of 
gypsum/pyrite/liming/dolomite, sprinkler sets and w ater carrying pipes to 
encourage farmers to grow pulses on a large scale.

1230.SHRI O.T. LEPCHA: Will the Minister of CONSUME R AFFAIRS, 
FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government propose to formulate any special  programme and 
scheme for providing foodgrains to the poor living in hilly/tribal/backward 
areas of the country particularly in the North Eastern Region; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor; and 
(c) the details of various schemes being implemented at  present by 
Government in the country? 
THE MINISTER OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC 
DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SHARAD PAWAR): (a) and (b) The G overnment 
has introduced the Village Grain Banks Scheme to pr ovide safeguard against 
starvation during the period of natural calamities in food scarce areas which 
cover people living in tribal areas, inaccessible h illy areas, drought prone 
areas and the hot and cold desert areas. Details of  the scheme are given in 
Statement (See below). 
(cj Apart from the Village Grain Banks Scheme, Gove rnment of India has 
been allocating foodgrains for people living under Below Poverty Line 
(BPL), Above Poverty Line.(APL) and Antyodaya Anna Yojana (AAY) 
under Targeted Public Distribution System and vario us other following 
Welfare Schemes: 
1.   Mid day Meal, (administered by Ministry of Human Resource, 
Development).

[9 March, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
2. Wheat Based Nutrition Programme and Nutrition Progr amme for 
Adolescent girls (administered by Ministry of Woman  and Child 
Development). 
3. Sampoorna Gramin Rpjgar Yojana (SGRY) and Special C omponent 
of SGRY (administered by Ministry of Rural Developm ent) and 
Annapurna Scheme. 
Statement  
Village Grain Banks Scheme  
• A Centrally Sponsored Scheme of Grains Banks in Tri bal villages 
was launched during 1996-97 by the Ministry of Trib al Affairs in 11 
States. During 1996-97 to 2004-05 Ministry of Triba l Affairs 
released Rs. 10.26 crores for establishing 4858'Gra in Banks. Now 
the scheme has been transferred to the Ministry of Food and Public 
Distribution. 
• The revised Village Grain Bank Scheme for establish ment of Grain 
Banks in chronically food scarce areas was approved  by Ministry of 
Finance on 15.2.2006 for the year 2005-06 and 2006- 07 subject to 
its evaluation in the 11th Plan. 
• The main objective of the scheme to provide safegua rd against 
starvation during the period of natural calamity or  during lean 
season. 
• The grain banks are to be set up in food scarce are as like the drought 
prone areas, the hot and cold desert areas, tribal areas and the 
inaccessible hilly areas. 
• The revised scheme envisages inclusion of all willi ng BPL/AAY 
families in the villages which will be identified b y the State 
Government in food deficit areas. The quantity to b e lent and the 
period of repayment will be decided by the Group th emselves. To 
ensure recovery of grains lent, it is proposed to t ie up the scheme 
with the entitlement of the members under TPDS. 
• Village Panchayat/Gram Sabha, Self Help Group or NG Os etc. 
identified by the State Government shall be eligible for running the 
135 

RAJYA SABHA [9 March, 2007] 
Grain Banks. Each such Executive Committee will have a Woman 
as its member. 
• A provision of Rs. 20.20 crores was made for 2005-0 6 (Plan) by 
Planning Commission out of which an amount of Rs. 1 9.76 crores 
was sanctioned for the establishment for 3282 grain  banks in the 
States of Andhra Pradesh, Orissa, Chhattisgarh, Mad hya Pradesh, 
Jharkhand, Tripura and Meghalaya. A provision of Rs . 50.00 crores 
has been made for 2006-07 out of which Rs. 49.40 cr ores has been 
sanctioned for the establishment of 7832 Grain Bank s in the States 
of Uttar Pradesh, Assam, Sikkim, Himachal Pradesh, Gujarat, West 
Bengal, Nagaland, Andhra Pradesh, Uttaranchal, Chha ttisgarh and 
Maharashtra so far. 
• The estimated cost of setting up one grain bank is as follows:

the State Government) 
c) Training expenses for trainers and trainees. Rs. 1400/-per bank.

Bogus ration cards  
1232. SHRI MOTIUR RAHMAN: 
SHRI KAMAL AKHTAR: 
Will the Minister of CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUB LIC 
DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the State Governments have been asked to la unch a drive to 
cancel bogus ration cards usurping ration articles meant for poor people; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the outcome of the drive; and 
(c) the number of complaints received against the irreg ularities committed 
by FPSs and KOD (Kerosene Oil Depot) holders during  the last three years 
and the action taken thereon? 
THE MINISTER OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC 
DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SHARAD PAWAR): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. 
Consequent upon State Food Ministers/Food Secretari es Conference held on 
29.3.2006 and Five Regional Conferences, a Nine Poi nts Action Plan was 
chalked out to check the diversion of foodgrains. O ne of the points was to 
undertake a campaign for Review of BPL/AAY lists, t o eliminate the ghost 
ration cards. Some of the States/UTs have completed  the drive and others are 
in the process of undertaking the drive. In the dri ve the respective State/UT 
has reviewed the ration cards to eliminate the bogus cards, if any. 
(c) The PDS is operated under the joint responsibil ity of the Central and 
State Governments. The Central Government has taken  the responsibility for 
procurement, storage, transportation and bulk alloc ation of foodgrains, etc. 
The responsibility for effectively distributing the  same to the consumers 
through the network of Fair Price Shop (FPSs) lies with the State 
138 

[9 March, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
Governments. The State Governments are responsible for identification of 
beneficiaries, issue them ration cards and distribu te foodgrains through a vast 
network of 4.89 lacs Fair Price Shops (FPSs) scatte red all over the country. 
In such a vast network, chances of irregularities c annot be ruled out. 
However, whenever a complaint is received by the Ce ntral Government, it is 
forwarded to the concerned State Government for inv estigation and 
necessary remedial action. 
The Section 8 of the PDS (Control) Order, 2001 stip ulates the directions 
of monitoring the PDS system while Section 9 deals with the penalties for 
contravenes any provision of the Order. 
The action taken under clauses 8 and 9 of the PDS ( Control) Order, 2001 
by the State Governments/UT Administrations during the last three years is 
given in the Statement.

1235. SHRI SYED AZEEZ PASHA: Will the Minister of C ONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to  state: 
(a) whether Government have any intention of doing way with the futures 
trading which is playing havoc with the lives of co mmon men of this country 
by causing immense price rise; 
(b) whether Government have any specific plan of action  that can correct 
the defective system of futures trading; and 
(c) whether Government have done a thorough study into the factors that 
cause recurring price rise due to persistent shorta ge of perishable 
commodities of everyday use like onions and other vegetables? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI 
TASLIMUDDIN): (a) In the context of discussion rega rding whether and.to 
what extent futures trading has contributed to pric e rise in agricultural 
commodities in recent times, the Government has set  up an Expert 
Committee on 2-3-07 under the Chairmanship of Profe ssor Abhijit Sen, 
Member, Planning Commission to study, inter alia, the extent of impact, if 
any, of futures trading on wholesale and retail pri ces of agricultural 
commodities. 
Forward Markets Commission (FMC) which is the Regul ator for 
commodity futures trading under the provisions of t he Forward Contracts 
(Regulation) Act, 1952, vide letter dated 23.01.2007 has directed the three 
National Exchanges, namely (i) Multi Commodity Exch ange of India Ltd., 
(ii) National Commodity & Derivatives Exchanges Ltd ., (iii) National Multi 
Commdity Exchange of India Ltd. to delist all contr acts of tur and urad and 
to close out all outstanding positions in all tur a nd urad contracts at the 
closing price on 23.01.2007. FMC has also stated th at no further contract 
shall be launched without its prior approval, and p ermission already granted 
to launch contracts in urad and tur stand withdrawn. 
Besides, FMC has on 27.2.2007 directed all the thre e National Exchanges 
that no new wheat and rice contracts be launched. I n the letter to the 
Exchanges, FMC has stated that permission already g ranted for yet to be 
launched contracts stands revoked and that in respe ct of running contracts in 
these commodities no new position should be allowed  to be taken. Only 
squaring up positions should be allowed.

(b) FMC has prescribed various regulatory measures such  as limit on open 
position, daily margins, limit on daily price varia tion etc. to ensure orderly 
trading in the futures market. Besides, the Governm ent has introduced 
Forward Contracts (Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2006  in the Lok Sabha on 
21.03.2006. The Bill, inter alia, seeks to enhance the regulatory powers of 
FMC in order to empower it to regulate the Commodit y Futures Market in a 
more effective manner.

such as seasonality of production, perishability, exports etc.

(a) the number of people benefited in different States from Antyodaya

(b) the details of the amount of foodgrains lifted unde r this scheme, State-
wise during the last two years; 
(c) whether the fixed quantity of foodgrains is indeed reaching to the

out this; 
(d) whether the different State Governments have receiv ed complaints 
regarding irregularity in the foodgrains distributi on system and if so, the

THE MINISTER OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC 
DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SHARAD PAWAR): (a)AStatement is annexed as 
per Statement-I (See below). 
(b) A Statement is annexed as per Statement-ll (See below). 
(c) Programme Evaluation Organization of Planning Commi ssion (PEO) 
and ORG Marg, New Delhi have conducted studies on P erformance 
Evaluation of Targeted Public Distribution System ( TPDS) and Evaluation 
study of TPDS and Antyodaya Anna Yojana (AAY) respectively. 
In their March, 2005 report, the PEO has reported t hat the Foodgrains 
leakage (as a percentage of offtake of BPL quota) t hrough ghost card is 
16.67% and at Fair Price Shop is 19.71% (all India basis). The main reasons 
for leakages are that implementation of TPDS is pla gued by targeting errors, 
prevalence of ghost cards and unidentified househol ds and siphoning off of 
foodgrains from the supply chain. 
As per the September, 2005 report of the ORG Centre  for Social 
Research, New Delhi diversion of wheat and rice is 53.3% and 39% 
respectively at the all India level. 
(d) and (e) The PDS is operated under the joint res ponsibility of the 
Central and State Governments. The Central Governme nt has taken the 
responsibility for procurement, storage, transporta tion and bulk allocation 
of foodgrains, etc The responsibility for effective ly distributing the same to 
the consumers through the network of Fair Price Sho ps (FPSs) lies with 
the State Governments. The State Governments are re sponsible for 
identification of  beneficiaries, issue them ration  cards and distribute 
foodgrains through Fair Price Shops (FPSs) scattere d all over the country. 
The chances of irregularities can not be ruled out.  However, when ever a 
complaint is received by the Central-Government, it  is forwarded to the 
concerned State Government for necessary remedial action. 
The PDS Control (Order) 2001 stipulates periodical review of functioning 
of the PDS by the State Governments and to furnish the outcome thereof. 
These reports are examined by the Central Governmen t and necessary 
instructions in consonance with the order are issue d to the State 
Governments from time to time. The Government of In dia are also holding 
National/Regional Level Conferences with the State Food Ministers and 
Food Secretaries from time to time to ensure smooth working of the PDS.

Expansion of AAY in Andhra Pradesh  
1237. SHRI NANDI YELLAIAH: Will the Minister of CON SUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to  state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that the Society for elimination of rural 
poverty has estimated on the basis of the World Ban k criteria that in Andhra 
Pradesh 23,84,535 families are at the risk of hunger; 
(b) if so, whether it is fact that so far only 10,34,54 5 families in rural 
areas have been covered under the Antyodaya Anna Yojana; and 
(c) if so, the details of the work-plan of Government t o cover the left over 
families under the next expansion of Antyodaya Anna Yojana? 
THE MINISTER OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC 
DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SHARAD PAWAR): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) No, Sir. As reported by the State Government of  Andhra Pradesh, 
13.68 lakh families in rural areas are covered unde r the Antyodaya Anna 
Yojana as on date. 
(c) The allocation of foodgrains under TPDS is made  on the basis of 
number of household estimated on the basis of pover ty estimates of the 
Planning Commission for 1993-94 projected on the po pulation projection of 
Registrar General as on 1.3.2000 or the number of r ation cards issued by the

throughout the country and can not be altered for any State in isolation.

Damage to environment due to global warming  
1238. SHRI SHANTARAM LAXMAN NAIK : Will the Ministe r of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether any assessment of damage to environment  in the country has 
been done on account of global warming; 
159 

RAJYA SABHA    [9 March, 2007] 
(b) whether global warming is likely to affect mons oon, winter and 
summer seasons; and 
(c) if so, in what manner? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMEN T 
AND FORESTS (SHRI NAMO NARAIN MEENA): (a) to (c) A preliminary 
assessment of impacts and vulnerability due to proj ected climate change in 
key sectors such as water, agriculture, forestry, e cosystems, coastal zones, 
health, energy and infrastructure has been undertak en. The projected climate 
change scenarios indicate increase in and variable trend of both rainfall and 
temperature into 21st century. It is projected that  quantity of surface run off 
due to climate change would reduce and vary across the various river basins. 
The initial analysis has revealed that climate chan ge may have adverse 
effects in terms of severity of droughts and intens ity of floods in various 
parts of the country. Increase in C0 2 concentration; increase in temperature 
and variable distribution of rainfall show a mixed projection of yields of 
various crops across the regions. No definite trend s have yet been 
established. Forest types in India seem to be highl y vulnerable to the 
projected changes in climate. Coastal areas are als o vulnerable to climate 
variability in varying degrees. 
The Government of India is seized of the various co ncerns that may arise 
due to climate change. The existing legislative and  policy framework in 
various sectors of concern, together with programme s which target 
conservation of rivers, improvement of urban air qu ality, enhanced 
forestation, promote renewable energy technologies and energy efficiency 
etc., contribute to addressing climate change issues.

Review of the steps taken to protect tigers  
1244.  SHRI KALRAJ MISHRA: 
SHRI KRISHAN LAL BALMIKI: 
Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be ple ased to 
state: 
(a) whether any review of the steps taken to protec t and promote tigers in 
different national parks, reserves and sanctuaries in the country, following the 
special surveys undertaken at the behest of the Pri me Minister's two years 
back has since been made; 
• (b) if so, the increase or decrease in tiger popu lation during the period, 
sector-wise; and 
(c) the steps being taken in that direction in the light of such surveys and 
reviews? 
166 

[9 March, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMEN T 
AND  FORESTS (SHRI NAMO NARAIN MEENA): (a) Yes, Sir. Pro ject 
Tiger has been reviewed by the Tiger Task Force con stituted by the National 
Board for Wildlife, Chaired by the Hon'ble Prime Mi nister. The Ministry of 
Environment & Forests is implementing the urgent re commendations of the 
said Task Force for strengthening tiger conservatio n which, inter-alia, 
includes the recent amendment to the Wildlife (Prot ection) Amendment Act 
for constituting the National Tiger Conservation Au thority (NTCA) and the 
Wildlife Crime Control Bureau. The NTCA has already  come into force 
w.e.f. 4th Septermber, 2006. Apart from above, all the Tig er Reserverhave 
been evaluated by a panel of independent experts ba sed on a set of criteria 
(45) developed by the World Commission on Protected  Areas, as adapted for 
Indian conditions. The evaluation has been peer-rev iewed by the 
International Union for Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources 
(IUCN). Both the assessment as well as peer-review have been placed in both 
the Houses of Parliament. 
(b) The process of All India estimation of tigers, copr edators and prey 
animals using the refined methodology, as approved by the Tiger Task 
Force, is ongoing in collaboration with the Wildlif e Institute of India. The 
said process on completion, would indicate the stat us of tiger population, its 
copredators, prey animals and habitat in the countr y. 
(c) The steps taken at the Government of India for cons ervation of tigers 
is at Statement. 
Statement  
Several milestone initiatives have been taken by the Government in the recent 
past for tiger conservation which are as below:  
1. Strengthening of anti-poaching activities, includin g special 
strategy for monsoon patrolling, by providing fundi ng support to 
Tiger Reserve States, as proposed by them, for depl oyment of anti-
poaching squads involving ex-army personnel/home gu ards, apart 
from workforce comprising of local people, in addit ion to 
strengthening of communication/wireless facilities. 
2. Implementation of the urgent recommendations of the  Tiger Task 
Force constituted by the National Board for Wildlife chaired by 
167 

RAJYA SABHA [9 March, 2007] 
the Hon'ble Prime Minister, which, inter alia, include Amendment 
of the Wild life (Protection) Act, 1972 for creatin g the National 
Tiger Conservation Authority and the Tiger and Othe r Endangered 
Species Crime Control Bureau. 
3. The National Tiger Conservation Authority has been constituted 
with effect from 4.9.2006, which would strengthen t iger 
conservation by, inter alia, ensuring normative standards in tiger 
reserve management, preparation of reserve specific  tiger 
conservation plan, laying down annual/audit report before 
Parliament, constituting State level Steering Commi ttees under the 
Chairmanship of Chief Ministers and establishment o f Tiger 
Conservation Foundation. 
4. Assessment of tiger habitat status in the country a t Taluka 
amplification in the Geographical Information Syste m (GIS) 
domain in collaboration with the Wild life Institute of India. 
5. Comparative appraisal of forest cover status in and  around tiger 
reserves (upto a radial distance of 10 kms.), in co llaboration with 
the Forest Survey of India for evolving reserve spe cific restorative 
strategies involving local people in the peripheral/buffer areas. 
6. Assessment of tiger reserves by a panel of independ ent experts 
based on 45 parameters, adapted from the framework of the World 
Commission on Protected Areas, which has been peer reviewed by 
the International Union for Conservation of Nature and Natural 
Resources (IUCN) and laid in the Parliament. 
7. Refinement of the All India Tiger Estimation proces s (including 
other prominent prey and predators apart from habit at monitoring) 
in collaboration with the Wild life Institute of India. 
8. Bilateral initiatives with neighbouring tiger range countries. 
9. Providing funding support for eco-development aroun d core areas 
of tiger reserve to foster inclusive management and  taking 
initiatives for evolving a set of eco-tourism guide lines to benefit 
local people. 
10.    Taking initiatives for enhancing the village  relocation package 
through a professional agency. 
168 

[9 March, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
Apart from the above, other initiatives taken by the Government for wild life 
conservation are as below:  
11. Legal protection has been provided to wild animals against hunting 
and commercial exploitation under the provisions of  the Wild life 
(Protection) Act, 1972. 
12. Several rare and endangered species of wild animal have been 
included in the Scheduled of Wild life (Protection)  Act, 1972, 
thereby giving it highest degree of protection. 
13. The Wild life (Protection) Act, 1972 has been amend ed and made 
more stringent. The punishment in cases of offences  has been 
enhanced. The Act also provides for forfeiture of a ny equipment, 
vehicle or weapon that has been used for committing  any wild life 
offence. 
14. Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) has been empo wered under 
the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 to apprehend an d prosecute 
wildlife offenders. 
15. Government of India has set up Regional and Sub-reg ional Offices 
for wildlife preservation in major export and trade  centers of the 
country to prevent smuggling of wild animals and their products. 
16. Financial and technical help is provided to the Sta tes under various 
Centrally Sponsored Schemes, viz. Project Tiger, Project Elephant 
and Development of National Parks and Sanctuaries f or enhancing 
the capacity and infrastructure of the States for p roviding effective 
protection to wild animals. 
17. A National Wildlife Action Plan 2002-2016 was adopt ed by the 
Indian Board for Wild life under the chairmanship o f Prime 
Minister in January, 2002. The plan outlines the st rategy for 
conservation and protection of wild life in the country. 
18. Government of India is a signatory to many internat ional 
conventions concering biodiversity conservation and  control of 
illegal trade in wild flora and fauna. 
19. Bilateral agreements have been signed with Nepal an d Republic of 
China for controlling trans-boundary illegal trade in wild life. 
169

20.    A Global Tiger Forum of Tiger Range Countries has been created for

Delhi, Mumbai, Pune, Bangalore, Chennai and Kanpur; 
* Introduction of cleaner fuels like Compressed Natur al Gas (CNG) 
and Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) in selected cities;

Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNF CCC) and Kyoto 
Protocol, and various partnerships with other count ries under the UNFCCC. 
While India does not have any Green House Gas (GHG)  abatement 
commitments under the Kyoto Protocol, a range of po licies and programs 
taken up help mitigate climate change. These include— 
* Improving energy efficiency & conservation as well setting up of 
Bureau of Energy Efficiency 
* Power sector reforms 
* Promoting hydro and renewable energy 
* Promotion of clean coal technologies 
* Coal washing & efficient utilization of coal 
* Afforestation and conservation of forests 
* Reduction of gas flaring

* Encouraging Mass Rapid Trnasport systems 
* Environmental quality management

1249. SHRI M.V. MYSURA REDDY Will the Minister of

Protection Act, 1994 with a new Notification in 2006;

replete with inconsistencies violating constitution al provisions and several 
Acts of the Parliament, like-ignored mandate of 73r d and 74th constitutional 
amendments, ignored local bodies, stultifies the ri ghts of citizens under 
Article 21 of the Constitution of India, makes seri ous inroads into the powers

which no provision is made; and

of the country?

Notification on Environment Impact Assessment (EIA)  on 14th September, 
2006 replacing the earlier Environment Impact Asses sment Notification, 
1994.

Notification, 2006. The Notification is a "Subordin ate Legislation" and 
therefore, as per Parliamentary Procedure, after its, publication in the Gazette 
of India on 14th September, 2006, an authenticated copy of the Notification 
was laid on the Table of both the Houses of Parliament. 
After holding extensive consultations with relevant  stakeholders over a 
period of one year, a draft Notification on the rev ised Environmental 
Clearance Process was notified on September 15,2005  inviting objections/ 
suggestions from the public within sixty days. Afte r due consideration of all

notified the final Notification on 14th September, 2006 superceding the EIA 
Notification, 1994.

the State Governments for bearing the additional ex penditure required for 
providing logistic support to the various Authoriti es and Committees to be 
constituted as per the Notification. The Notificati on provides for 'Public

Produce Market Committee (APMC) Acts, the State Gov ernments are 
empowered to set up markets on agricultural commodi ties in notified areas. 
The farmer is restricted from entering into direct contract with any 
manufacturers as the produce is regulated to be can alized through licensed 
traders, and regulated markets. These restrictions have been found to be 
acting as disincentive to farmers, trade and indust ry. The development of 
alternative competitive market would provide freedo m to farmers to sell their 
produce in the markets providing better prices/serv ices. With a view to 
remove these constraints and to create an integrate d internal market by 
bringing uniformity in APMC Act, the Ministry of Ag riculture has 
formulated a Model Law namely "Agricultural Produce  Marketing 
(Development and Regulation) Act, 2003" and circula ted to all States/Union 
Territories for bringing changes in their respectiv e laws dealing with 
agricultural markets. Since agriculture marketing i s a State subject, it is for 
the State Governments to amend the APMC Act as suited to them. 
The State Governments of Madhya Pradesh, Himchal Pr adesh, Punjab, 
Sikkim, Nagaland, Andhra Pradesh, Rajasthan, Chhatt isgarh,. Orissa, 
Chandigarh, Arunachal Pradesh and Maharashtra have made amendments on 
the major areas of reforms suggested in the Model L aw and Haryana, 
Karnataka, National Capital Territory of Delhi, Utt ar Pradesh and Gujarat 
made partial reforms. In the State of Tamil Nadu, A PMC Act already 
provides

Gangmen died on duty  
1322. SHRI SANJAY RAUT : Will the Minister of RAILW AYS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) the number of gangmen died on duty due to train acc idents, while 
actually repairing the railway tracks in the year 2 005-06 and how many died 
in the current year; 
(b) what precautions his Ministry proposes to save the precious life of 
gangmen while repairing railway track; 
(c) how much compensation is paid to each gangman who d ies, while 
working on railway track; and 
(d) whether his Ministry give employment to one member of family of 
gangman who dies in the accident? 
249 

RAJYA SABHA [9 March, 2007] 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS 
(SHRI R. VELU): (a) 183 Nos. Gangmen died on duty t o train accidents in 
the year 2005-06 and 198 Nos. died in the current y ear while actually 
repairing the railway tracks. 
(b) The following precautions are taken to contain accidents at work spots 
to save the precious Iives of gangmen while repairing Railway track:— 
(i)   Introduction of visibility reflective safety jackets for the gangmen 
working on the track during the night. 
(ii)   Provision of remote operated hooters to give  warning to working 
gangmen at all work sites. 
(iii) Mobile phone or Walkie-Talkie sets wherever n ecessary are being 
provided at work sites. 
(iv)   Posting of look-out men at all work sites where visibility is poor. 
(v)   At locations where night working is unavoidab le, proper lighting 
arrangements are being made. 
(vi)   Provision of torches to all night Patrolmen/Watchmen. 
(vii) Welding works and other important tracks work s that require line 
block are being carried out under traffic line block. 
(viii) Posting of competent Supervisors at all works sites to ensure safety. 
(ix) In case of line, block works such as renewal o f points and crossing 
etc., Caution orders are being issued for the train s passing on 
adjoining track to give whistle freely to alert the working gangmen. 
(c) As per sections 124 and 124-Aof the Railways Act, C ompensation is 
payable to the dependents of passengers including R ailway men on duty who 
are killed as a result of passenger train accidents  or other untoward incidents. 
The amount of compensation payable in case of death  is Rs. 4 lakhs. 
Gangmen being Railway employees are entitled to com pensation under the 
Workman's Compensation Act. However, they can claim  compensation only 
under one of the above mentioned two Acts. 
(d) Yes, Sir. Railways give employment to one member of  family of 
gangman who dies in the accident.

Demand to amend anti-defection law  
SHRI SHANTARAM LAXMAN NAIK(Goa): Sir, the Tenth Sch edule of the 
Constitution of India, which is popularly known as "Anti-defection" law has 
been amended to ban defection of Members of parliam ent and State 
Assemblies and Councils. Undoubtedly, menace of def ection has been 
curbed to a great extent on account of the amendmen t. But, there are those 
who do not hesitate to betray the political parties  on the pedestal of which 
they built their careers. As the law stands today, if a Member of a political 
party defies the directions given to the Member in favour of the proposal of 
the party in respective Houses, no doubt, the Member can be disqualified. 
However, if the Member openly associates with other  political parties 
and/or citizens, the political party of which he/sh e is a Member or makes 
defamatory allegation against its office bearers or  other leaders the political 
party cannot take any action except to expel such M ember from the party. In 
this case, the Member becomes an unattached Member of the concerned 
House. He becomes a free bird, retaining his Member ship, all facilities 
atached to it with full freedom to criticise the po litical party of which he/ she 
was a member until recently, openly to utter embarrassment of the party. 
It is therefore, necessary that the Tenth Schedule should be further 
amended to disqualify all the Members who openly as sociate with other 
political parties and/or openly criticise the party , its office bearers and other 
leaders with defamatory Statements. Such actions on the part of a Member of 
a political party amounts to voluntary giving up me mbership of that political 
party and should be treated as such. 
Demand for legislation for social security snd employment          
guarantee for the workers of unorganised sector  
SHRI KARNENDU BHATTACHARJEE (Assam): Sir, I rise to  draw the 
attention of the Government to the need for a proper legislation for social 
265 

RAJYA SABHA [9 March, 2007] 
security and employment guarantee for the unorganis ed sector. The 
unorganised sector consititutes 93 per cent of the total work force of the 
country which are deprived of their rights. Recentl y, the unorganised sector 
held a rally in the capital city demanding a proper legisaltion for their rights. 
Nearly six decades after having attained freedom, t here is no law on 
minimum wages, medical facilities and pension for 4 0 crore workers in the 
informal sector, which, perhaps, is not proper on t he part of those who are at 
the helms of power. I think it will not be out of p lace to mention about setting 
up of a National Commission for inter-State migrant workers and enactment of 
a special law catering to the needs of agricultural  workers and setting aside at 
least three per cent of gross domestic product for social security for 
unorganised sector workers. 
I fear that creation of Special Economic Zones may lead to greater 
unemploymetn amongst farmers and agricultural labou rers. So, I urge upon 
the Government to go in for a legislation at the ea rliest possible so that the 
unorganised sector can be provided with social secu rity and guarantee for

WITH PRASAR BHARATI) BILL, 2007  
MR. DEPUTY CHAIRMAN: Now, we shall take up the Statutory 
Resolution regarding Sports Broadcasting Signals (Mandatory Sharing with 
Prasar Bharati) Ordinance, 2007. Shri Ram Jethmalani. Not here. Dr. Murli

.   move the Bill.

[9 March, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF PARLIAMENTARY AFFAIRS AND MINISTER OF 
INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING (SHRI PRIYARANJAN DASM UNSI): 
Sir, I move: 
"That the Bill to provide access to the largest num ber of listeners and 
viewers, on a free to air basis, of sporting events  of national importance 
through mandatory sharing of sports broadcasting si gnals with Prasar 
Bharati and for matters connected therewith or inci dental thereto, as 
passed by Lok Sabha, be taken into consideration." 
Sir, I may submit through you to the distinguished members of the House 
that since 1995 in Calcutta High court, in Delhi Hi gh Court and finally in the 
Supreme Court, there are enough number of petitions. I do not like to take the 
time of the House to read them one after another. T hese are pertaining to the 
position of the airwaves and the downlinking or upl inking policy of the Prasar 
Bharati. 
Sir, the Supreme Court held that the airwaves were the public property and 
later on gave directions to frame guidelines for do wnlinking and uplinking 
policy. Accordingly, Sir, the idea was mooted in 19 97 to bring a 
comprehensive broadcasting legislation in Parliamen t. Unfortunately, due to 
dissolution of the House, that could not take place . Although my distinguished 
predecessor, Sushma Swarajji, again tried to bring it as a Convergence Act, 
that also could not take place due to dissolution o f the House. At the end of 
the day, we planned to bring a comprehensive legisl ation on three counts. We 
shall discuss it with the stakeholders; the freedom  of expression and speech, 
and independence of the newspaper editors, and tele vision anchors will not 
be interfered; and there should not be a kind of re gulatory body where the 
Government take control of the media to oppose it. Therefore, Sir, our UPA 
Government adopted a policy that such a draft Bill should be discussed 
among all the stakeholders, not just once but ten t imes. We are in the process 
and hopefully, Sir, we will bring that comprehensiv e law very shortly. And I 
claim, Sir, today, on the floor of the House that the Bill that we will bring will be 
unparalleled in any democratic country in the world. 
Sir, in the meanwhile, we are caught in a bad situa tion. The guideline was 
supposed to be mooted in the law earlier. Since the  law could not take place, 
the guideline, after the directions of the court, w as prepared for downlinking 
and uplinking, especially the sports related matters. For that,

Prasar Bharati is broken. Prasar Bharati is now cle arly seen as an arm of the 
Government. If this is how the Prasar Bharath's goi ng to grow, then, the 
dream that one day Prasar Bharati will be autonomou s in the same way as 
the British Broadcasting Corporation, would be frus trated. There are 
absolutely no hopes of survival.

content owner has acquired the rights of broadcasti ng or telecasting in a 
particular normal contractual way. There was a time  when during the 
emergency, we put the word 'socialism' in the Pream ble of the Constitution. 
The Supreme Court judgement used to say that in vie w of the fact that 
socialism is the tenet in the Constitution, we inte rpret the law in a particular 
way. 
Sir, recently, in a case, the Supreme Court decided  that any officer who 
was suspended would not necessarily get the arrears  of pay, etc. The 
Supreme Court has said since the market economy is the basis of our 
economic policy, we give a judgement of this type. 
Now, nowhere 'socialism' is really the basic tenet,  even though it continues 
to be in the Preamble. Therefore, anybody who has a cquired the rights to 
telecast in a proper manner, to expropriate it by a  mere fiat of a notification or

say that the cricket matches of the World Cup are o f national importance. But

and we were coming on the top?

included to give relief to the common man. 
So, these are some of the measures. I feel that the  Government has failed 
to take effective measures. They lack long-term str ategy. What is going to 
happen? They have failed to take effective measures  whether it is 
implementing the Essential Commodities Act or it is  checking black-marketing 
and hoarding. These are some of the measures which the Government did 
not take properly. I urge upon the Government to th ink seriously and effective 
intervention by taking all these measures because o nly then we can give a 
little bit relief to the common man by checking the inflation in prices. 
The question was proposed.

[9 March, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
SHRI SHANTARAM LAXMAN NAIK (Goa): Sir, I do not agr ee with the 
contents of the resolution moved by my learned coll eague. Although I share 
his concern, and the entire House obviously, over t he inflationary tendencies 
being shown recently. I do not agree because he bla tantly blames the 
Government for, what he calls, failure of the Gover nment to check the inflation 
and steep rise in prices. This is not necessarily s o. In fact, it is like AIDS, still 
we don't know what the cause of AIDS are. If you ask economists what are the 
basic things which lead to price rise. You will get  4-5 versions. In other words, 
the science of determining price rise is not defini te. Therefore, to blatantly 
blame the Government is not justified, although we all share his concern over 
whatever is happening. But first thing I would like  to say that we have been 
rather a bit shy of using the Essential Commodities  Act. Everybody seems to 
be shy of using the Essential Commodities Act. When  certain things are very 
much know that in the entire economy hoarding takes  place to a large extent, 
not to use the Essential Commodities Act is not a g ood measure. Therefore, a 
rationale use of the Essential Commodities Act has to be done because 
artificial scarcities were created and are being cr eated at present. It is a well 
known thing. But how do you curb it? Earlier, when the Essential Commodities 
Act was in full force, even the smallest trader use d to display prices of 
commodities. There was a discipline at every consum er store. Even average 
common man used to go there to read the prices, in whatever local language. 
That was a deterrent. Deterrent punishment is there  for anybody hoarding or 
not displaying prices, etc. Therefore, in this vast  country of millions of people 
to allow things to go without being checked will no t be a good sign. It will not 
be a thing like free economy, free trade, etc. and keep aside the basic laws. 
Therefore, this aspect has to be looked into. Then,  in the interest of the 
common man we should also see that more items, even  like cooking oil, soap, 
etc. should be made available at reasonable prices through the public 
distribution system. Today on account of advertisem ents, costs of essential 
commodities, I do not say essential commodities tec hnically, but they are 
essential commodities, have risen far above the tru e price. A soap which 
would have cost Rs. 5/-costs Rs. 15, only because w e seen on television 
advertisement, actors and actrersses showing a part icular brand of soap. The 
same is the case with palm oil and other things. Therefore, if you want to serve 
the common

Another aspect is this. The fallout of rising price s is there politically also. It

I feel if people judge Governments really on econom ic issues, we should not

SHRI TAPAN KUMAR SEN (West Bengal): Mr. Deputy Chai rman, Sir, I 
rise to support the Resolution moved by my esteemed  colleague. Sir, I don't 
blame this Government alone for this run away infla tion because the credit or 
discredit of the present kind of price situation sh ould not be, at least, wholly 
owned by any particular Government. The whole infla tionary situation is the 
result of pursuit of a particular brand of economic  philosophy, a particular 
brand of economic policy regime which was being fol lowed even prior to the 
period of this UPA Government. The same policy of r elying everything on 
market, relying everything on the solution being of fered by automatic 
operation of market, has given rise to serious stru ctural problem called 
inflation. I don't consider this inflation to be on e of cyclical nature-sometimes 
up and sometimes down. Gradually, the whole charact er, the manner the 
things are taking shape, it is taking the shape of a serious structural problem. 
I blame definitely this Government about the respon se to the serious situation 
that has arisen at the grassroot level because of the inflation, the manner they 
proposed to address this inflationary situation, th e condition which has 
seriously put the majority of the population in our country in utter distress. 
What they are suggesting-even as expressed in the B udget Speech, as 
expressed in the President's Address, and, as repli ed by the hon. Prime 
Minister Yesterday in this House-is that all steps are taken. What steps are 
being taken only to address the money supply? What is the philosophy 
behind that? Is that the diagnosis that this inflat ion has taken place because 
there is too much money in the market, too much mon ey chasing too less a 
quantum of goods. So, the monetary intervention is to see that liquidity is less 
in the market on the one hand, and, on the other ha nd, supply side is 
managed by increasing indiscriminate Import. A day or two before, also in 
reply to a specific question raised in this House, this

disincentive to our rural economy, which, unfortuna tely, represents the 
majority of our population. Their purchasing power is already going down. 
There is too much money in the market. Yes, Sir, th e statistics will show that 
there is too much money in the market but that is i n the hands of the few. 
There is not too much of money in the hands of the 70 per cent of the 
population. Yes, there is too much money in the mar ket and that money has 
to be contained, but not by your so called monetary  measures, which you are 
prescribing through your Budget. There are ways and  means to contain that 
money, and, those ways and means must be unhesitati ngly utilized. That too 
much money in the market cannot be contained by you r monetary measures. 
On the other hand, those who are not having purchas ing power are dying 
despite your Vidarbha package in Maharashtra. I am grateful to the 
Agriculture

[9 March, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
Minister that he admitted this reality on the quest ion raised in this House 
today morning regarding suicide by farmers that the  situation of our farmers is 
really a matter of concern. More than sixty per cen t of our population in the 
rural economy is not getting the facility of irriga tion and credit. They are 
having serious credit problem Majority is still in the hands of the Sahukars, 
moneylenders. On the other hand, sixty per cent of our population are striving 
on that economy, that rural economy. On the one han d, you are putting up 
disincentives an agriculture everyday; on the other  hand, you are talking 
about improved agricultural productivity. No elemen t of watershed 
management, no element of irrigation, no element of  bank credit can change 
the situation unless agriculture is made remunerati ve, and, our peasants get 
remunerative prices. 
And as a result, what is happening? The purchasing power of people is 
going down. People are committing suicide. The pove rty level is increasing, 
although official claims say that it is declining. But in reality, it is increasing. In 
reality there is a compression of demand in rural e conomy. Whatever demand 
is there in the market, it is looked upon as excess  demand, and we go in for 
all monetary intervention to address that excess de mand situation. I think we 
are in a vicious circle of utter confusion. I must not say confusion, because if 
the policy is aimed at benefiting a few at the cost  of millions, it ought to go in 
that direction in addressing the inflationary situa tion, and that is precisely 
taking place. 
Sir, I would also like to draw your attention and, through you, the attention 
of the Government towards another basic important i ssue that you need to 
address if this situation has to be seriously addre ssed and people have to be 
given relief. Your Public Distribution System must be strengthened. Even 
yesterday, our hon. Prime Minister also admitted th e necessity of that. Even 
today, hon. Agriculture Minister admitted the neces sity of that. But in your 
Budget, what have you done? So far as the Public Di stribution System is 
concerned, there is only 6.2 per cent increase in a llocation in the food 
subsidy. And that 6.2 per cent in the face of an in flation rate of more than 6 
per cent means a negative and absolute decline in t he real allocation for the 
Public Distribution System. You are admitting that the growth should be 
inclusive. You are admitting that in the face of in flation, the Public Distribution 
System must be strengthened. On the other hand, you  are allocating only 6,2 
per cent. You are cutting a crude joke to the major ity of the population that 
you are curing or addressing the inflationary 
327 

RAJYA SABHA [9 March, 2007] 
situation. What have you suggested in view of addre ssing the situation in the 
Employment Guarantee Scheme? Your real allocation h as increased to the 
tune of 3.5 per cent Again, it is an absolute decli ne if you take inflation rate 
into consideration. From 200 to 330 districts in th e rural areas who are facing 
the scourage of inflation most, who are committing suicide in a big way, only 
3.5 per cent increase in the allocation. That is we ll below half of the inflation

say that there must be growth; growth is hot an end  by itself; and, at the same

bytes in electronic media and nothing else. Because  your all means of

doing this unknowingly. My saying is that you are d oing it knowingly and this 
attitude is reflected by the Government's own state ment. While replying on the 
President's Address, the Government says that the inflation is to be addressed 
but the growth impulse of the country's economy sho uld not be affected. 
Addressing inflation, addressing the maladies being faced by 60 percent of the 
population will effect the growth impulse of the ec onomy! If this be the 
preception, the Government's addressing the inflati on is bound to go in other 
direction. Sir, through you, I want to request the Government that please 
retrace your steps from this faulty pursuit of addr essing inflation. Otherwise, 
we will be facing and the country will be facing a serious situation. To

Parliamentary debates. "Any Government worth its sa lt, any Government 
which is concerned about the poor of this country, any Government which 
recognises that 30 per cent of the people are below  the poverty line, any 
Government which is sensitive, any Government which  has some heart must 
place inflation control number one on the agenda. T his Government has failed 
to do that." Quotation is over. If the Government f ails to do that, it will be 
paying a price for that today or tomorrow. Up to po rtion I have quoted, it is 
spoken by our present Finance Minister, Mr. Chidamb aram, in Lok Sabha on 
3rd December 1998, as a Member of the Opposition. I  want to repeat the 
same statement. Please don't create a situation and  land in a situation of 
paying a heavy price. Please correct yourself. By s trengthening the Public 
Distribution System and by directly checking the

situation. How Rs. 1,25,000 crores, as on date, are the arrears of taxes, direct

this Resolution which is a vital one, which is very  timely, and which focuses 
on a very important issue which affects the whole c ountry. I do not intend to 
apportion blame on anyone. I have no pretence to sa y that I know the 
solution to the problem, but I just want to put bef ore you and this august 
House that this problem is a real one. We must acce pt initially and not feel 
shy of agreeing, whether it is the Government or wh ether it is the Opposition, 
that mahngai, steep rise in prices, is the real problem which is confronting the 
whole nation, particularly those who are BPL, those  who are SCs, those who 
are Tribals, those who are OBCs those who are the p oorest of the poor and 
wretched of the wretched. It affects them very badl y. Once we agree that 
problem is there, then there is  need for a solemn, thougtful discussion across 
party lines and then ultimately reach a solution. I f Rajya Sabha and Lok 
Sabha, these august Houses, are not able to find ou t a solution then debates 
are only oral exercises without producing any resul t. What happened in 
history can be a matter of interest, but it would n ot solve the present crisis.

statistics, there are 10 per cent families, at leas t, in the country where a 
person has to live on Rs. 9/- a day. There are 20 p er cent such families 
where a person has to live on Rs. 12/- a day. With that much budget, if it is

is there. A common man, who is below the poverty li ne, or the Aam adm of 
the country, does not understand the intricacies of  statistics of inflation 
because statistics, they say, are like bikini bathi ng suits. What they reveal is 
suggestive, but what they hide is vital. If inflati on rate has to be counted, let it 
be counted of those basic agricultural commodities without which a person 
cannot live and survive. Then, we will know really how much price rise has 
taken place. I am sure hardly will there be any per son, out of the one billion 
and ten crore population of this country, who would  put his hand up and say

frightening some people who have been traditionally  the enemies of the

MR. CHAIRMAN: Shri Su. Thirunavukkarasar. 
SHRI SU. THIRUNAVUKKARASAR (Madhya Pradesh); Sir, I thank you very

Changes in RGGVY and APDRP 
†*181. SHRI MOTILAL VORA: †† 
SHRI SATYAVRAT CHATURVEDI: 
Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Rajeev Gandhi Grameen Vidyutikaran Yojana ( RGGVY) and 
Accelerated Power Development and Reform Programme (APDRP) have not yielded 
desired results; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
††The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Shri Motilal Vora. 
5 

RAJYA SABHA [12 March, 2007] 
(c) whether Government are considering to bring about some changes in these 
schemes in order to make them more meaningful; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHIL KUMAR SHINDE): ( a) to 
(d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement  
(a) and (b) Rajiv Gandhi Grameen Vidyutikaran Yojan a (RGGVY) and 
Accelerated Power Development and Reform Programme (APDRP) have yielded 
the desired results. 
In the year 2005-06 under Rajiv Gandhi Grameen Vidyutikaran Yojana, 9819 
unelectrified villages were electrified against the  target of 10,000 villages and 
in 2006-07, as on 2.3.2007,22233 unelectrified villages have been electrified. 
Besides this, intensive electrification of 7413 alr eady electrified villages has 
also been completed. Franchisees are in place in 39113 villages already which 
is meant to ensure revenue sustainability. The revenue collection has increased 
with the installation of franchisees. 
As regards APDRP, its basic objectives are to reduc e Aggregate Technical 
and Commercial (AT&C) losses, improving quality of supply of power, 
increasing revenue collection and improving consumer satisfaction. The AT&C 
losses of the State distribution companies at national level were reduced from 
38.86% in 2001-02 to 33.83% for 2004-05. At town le vel, AT&C losses have 
been brought below 20 per cent in 212 APDRP towns in the country of which 169 
towns have brought AT&C losses below 15 percent. Overall commercial loss 
(without subsidy) of the distribution companies reduced from Rs. 29.331 crore 
during 2001-02 to Rs. 22,129 crore during 2004-05. The commercial loss in 
percentage of turnover has reduced from 36.55% in 2001-02 to 20.70% in 2004-
05. 
(c) and (d) The present approval is for the Phase-I of the scheme, RGGVY for years 
2005-06 and 2006-07 of the X-Plan. The scheme is under evaluation by the Planning 
Commission for its continuation in the Xl-Plan. 
The APDRP was approved by the Government for implementation during X 
Plan. The Ministry had constituted a Task Force hea ded by Shri P. Abraham, 
former Secretary, Government of India, to assess and analyse the current efforts 
under APDRP, suggestions made by various agencies 
6 

[12 March, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
and to suggest restructuring of the programme. The Task Force has submitted 
its report which is under consideration.

two very pertinent issues.

estimation made by the State Governments? There is a vast difference between 
the two. Now, if that is the case, this one-fifth a lso would be much lower than

confusion. If the State Government says that 1, 2 or 3 are BPL, we accept that

the capacity addition, particularly considering the illness of the poor people. You 
must be seeing, I have said a number of times in this House, that the country has a

more, but still I am not satisfied and

Schemes for girl education  
*183. DR. GYAN PRAKASH PILANIA: Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) what steps and which schemes, have been announced by Centre/ States to 
give fillip to girl students and also to encourage female education; 
(b) the funds sanctioned and achievements, made thereof, during the last 
three years in the country; 
(c) whether any quota has been reserved for girl students from primary to 
university level; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; and 
16 

[12 March, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
(e) the present status of female education in the country, State-wise? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI D. PURANDESWARI): (a) to (e) A Statement is 
laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement  
(a) The Ministry of Human Resource Development and its nodal 
organisations have undertaken several schemes to promote girls education in the 
country. The main schemes are listed below: 
Elementary Education 
(i) Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA) including National Programme for 
Education of Girls at Elementary Level (NPEGEL) as a sub 
component of Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan. 
(ii) Kasturba Gandhi Balika Vidyalayas (KGBVs). 
Secondary Education 
(i) Scholarship scheme being implemented by Central  Board of 
Secondary Education (CBSE) for single girl child. 
(ii) Full fee waiver to single girl child from class VI to XII in all Kendriya 
Vidyalayas. 
(iii) Scheme of assistance for Hostel facilities fo r girl students of

RAJYA SABHA [12 March, 2007] 
DR. GYAN PRAKASH PILANIA: Sir, through this questio n, I wanted to 
focus attention regarding the plight of female education in the country, a subject 
which has been dear to your own self. And, you will  recollect that when you 
were the Chief Minister of Rajasthan, you were the first person to start this 
campaign of female education there, and you had alw ays been emphasising 
that education to women is the first input for empo werment of women in the 
country. I would like to draw the attention of the hon. Minister, who has given a 
detailed statement, but has not touched the core qu estion which I had raised, 
namely, the scenario of female education and regard ing his evaluation as to 
where he stands. Does the hon. Minister appreciate that the dropout rate of 
girls, before reaching V standards is 28.57 per cen t; the dropout rate of girls, 
before reaching VIII standard is 52.9 per cent, and the dropout rate of girls, before 
reaching X standard, is 64.92 per cent. This is an alarming scenario of dropout 
of girls. Sir, I am raising this supplementary by drawing the attention of the House to 
certain statistics which he has not given in his re ply to the Question, but 
depending on the replies received from Starred Questions and other Questions in 
the Rajya Sabha, from where I have culled these figures... 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Let the Minister reply. 
SHRIMATI D. PURANDESWARI: Sir, definitely, we are a ll very much 
concerned about the dropout rates of girl child. As we all know, the dropout rate 
amongst girls is higher as they go to higher classe s. But there are various 
reasons for it. it is both social and economic reas ons that we need to take into 
consideration. When we take the reasons into consideration, these could be lack 
of accessibility to school, lack of transportation,  or, it could be teacher 
absenteeism which is actually reducing the interest  of children from going to 
school. But all these reasons have been taken into consideration, and we are 
working towards ensuring accessibility, the require d infrastructure, seeing to 
it the teachers are in place, so as to ensure that the girl children are brought back 
to school. We also have the alternative Innovative Education Scheme and the 
Education Guarantee Scheme which actually works or functions as the bridge 
school to ensure that these girl children, who are out of school, are brought back 
into the mainstream of education. So, it is not as if the Government is not doing 
anything. The Government is fully seized of it and it is, definitely, working 
towards ensuring that the girl child is brought back to school.

Skill Development Mission  
† *185. SHRI RAM JETHMALANI: 
DR. MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI: †† 
Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government have a proposa l to set up a Skill 
Development Mission in the country; 
(b) if so, the outlines of the proposal; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that additional measures are required to meet the 
requirement of skilled workers for the developing industries in the country; 
(d) if so, the reaction of Government thereto; and 
(e) by when the proposal for setting up of said mission  is likely to be 
implemented? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI MD. ALI ASHRAF FATMI): (a) to (e) A Statement is 
laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement  
(a) to (e) In his speech on the Independence Day, 2006, the Prime Minister 
referred to the imminent shortage of skilled employ ees for the booming 
economy and growing industry and announced the plan  of the Government to 
launch a Mission on Vocational Education to address  the skill deficit in our 
economy. Based on this announcement, a Task Force on Skill Development has 
been constituted by the Planning Commission to make  recommendations on 
how to meet the requirements of skilled

and beyond. The Task Force is also required to suggest the nature and scope of the 
Mission to carry out this mandate, and to recommend  additional measures to 
meet the requirement of skilled manpower. The Plann ing Commission has 
informed that the Task Force is expected to submit its report by end of March, 
2007.

Implementation of the Tribal Rights Bill  
*184. SHRI V. HANUMANTHA RAO: Will the Minister of TIRBAL 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have appointed a Committee of retired officials to 
suggest rules for implementing the Tribal Rights Bill; 
(b) the purpose of this Committee; 
(c) whether Government are facing a shortage of talent in framing rules; 
(d) if so, the steps proposed to fix a strict time limit of three months for the 
said Committee to be wound up; and 
(e) the measures proposed to evolve a balanced and sustainable set of rules; 
THE MINISTER OF TRIBAL AFFAIRS (SHRI P.R. KYNDIAH): (a) and 
(b) The Ministry of Tribal Affairs has constituted a Technical Support Group 
on 12.2.2007 for framing the draft rules for carrying out the provisions of the 
Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest 
Rights) Act, 2006. The Technical Support Group has 21 members consisting 
of reputed experts and officials from concerned Min istries/Departments. The 
experts include two retired Government officials. 
(c) No, Sir. 
(d) The Technical Support Group has been asked to prepare the draft rules 
within 3 month from the date of its constitution. 
(e) The Technial Support Group has been constituted wit h experts from 
different fields specifically to ensure that a balanced and sustainable set of rules 
is prepared. The Group will hold consultations with  State Governments/Union 
Territory Administrations and concerned experts before finalising the draft rules. 
Prior publication of the draft rules, as required under the Act, will also be done 
to elicit comments and suggestions of the public before the rules are finalised.

Power allotted to Madhya Pradesh  
†*187   MISS ANUSUIYA UIKEY: 
SHRIMATI MAYA SINGH: 
Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact thai 300 megawatt of elect ricity had been allotted 
to Madhya Pradesh from central power plants of east ern areas as on July, 
2002; 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
36 

[12 March, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) whether supply of power being made to the State has been reduced to 50 
megawatts; 
(c) if so, the reasons for reducing the power supply; and 
(d) by when the supply of power would be resumed as  per earlier 
allotment? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHIL KUMAR SHINDE): (a) Yes, 
Sir. 
(b) to (d) In view of less than anticipated growth in demand for power in the 
Eastern Region (ER), in earlier years, the unallocated power of NTPC stations in 
the ER as well as the shares temporarily surrendere d by ER constituents, had 
been allocated to States/UTs in other regions over the last few years. However, 
in recent years ER constituents have been demanding  repatriation of the 
power surrendered by them as well as allocation of unallocated power to them 
in view of the increase in their requirement. Conse quently, the allocation to 
States/UTs in other regions from the ER has been de creasing. Accordingly the 
allocation of ER power to Madhya Pradesh also got reduced to 50 MW. 
In November, 2006, following the sudden outage of R angahadi HEP and 
consequent shortage of power in Assam, 46 MW power from Eastern Region 
(ER) was allocated to Assam by reducing the allocat ions of beneficiaries of 
ER power, including about 4 MW from the allocation of Madhya Pradesh. 
In view of the foregoing the assistance to Madhya Pradesh from the central 
plants in the Eastern Region is not likely to be increased to the earlier level of 
300 MW.
